text: Differentiating common swine skin conditions: Greasy skin/Exudative Dermatitis (Staphylococcus infecting abraded skin) — starts as small, dark brown, greasy-looking patches around the face or legs that gradually spread to cover the whole body; can be fatal in severely affected piglets; prevent by avoiding wet, abrasive flooring (which causes knee lesions), careful teeth clipping, and disinfecting the sow's udder twice a day with iodine (a common infection reservoir); treatment (Amoxicillin LA, Lincomycin, or a disinfectant skin spray like TH4) has limited effectiveness. Erysipelas (bacterial, present on almost all farms, uncommon before 3 months old) — large diamond-shaped raised areas turning red then black (often palpable before visible), sometimes sudden death from septicemia/heart failure, very high fever (>41°C), and refusal to eat; can be vaccinated against in breeders (2 doses, 4 weeks apart, from 4 months, e.g. Ruvax); treat with Penicillin or Amoxicillin for 3–5 days. Mange (parasite) — red irritation mainly on the back and flanks, rubbing, and ear shaking with dark material inside the ear; prevent with routine Ivermectin every 3 months; treat with Ivermectin (1 ml/30 kg, twice within 2 weeks to match the 10–14 day parasite cycle, subcutaneous) or daily in feed for 7 days (the most effective method). Insect bites — red spots, skin irritation, blood loss, and poor growth; prevent by cleaning fly resting/breeding sites (waste feed, slurry crusts, wall cracks); treat with insecticide spray (Trichlorfon) on resting sites, Butox on animals every 2 months, and Dexamethasone for severe irritation or Amoxicillin if spots become infected. Sunburn — red, wet, painful skin with fever after sun exposure, potentially fatal if severe dehydration and body temperature above 42°C occur; prevent with shade; treat by spraying water on the pig to cool it, ensuring it drinks, and injecting Paracetamol (note: PRRS can look similar in fattening pigs but comes with swollen eyes, coughing, and reproductive problems in the herd). CSF (purple discoloration) — skin turns purple starting at the ears and tail, spreading to the snout, lower legs, belly, and back, with prolonged high fever (>40°C) and a drunken walk. Cyanosis (blue extremities): from Salmonellosis — typically around 12–14 weeks old, blue tail/ears/nose/feet, high fever, pneumonia/respiratory distress, foul-smelling diarrhea, in pigs under 6 months (prevent with hygiene/disinfection, avoid water baths once disease is present since they favor Salmonella; vaccines aren't useful; treat with TMP+Sulfa or Enrofloxacin, though resistance develops quickly) — or from PRRS ('Blue Ear Disease'), where blue ears are actually a rare, unreliable sign compared to the more telling signs of anorexia, fever, abortion, and weak/mummified piglets.
